name: Hybrid Immunity and Prior Infection Effects
anchorClaim: Individuals with both prior SARS-CoV-2 infection and vaccination (hybrid immunity) show measurably higher protection against reinfection or severe disease compared to vaccination alone, as reported in observational and cohort studies of vaccine effectiveness.
plainQuestion: Having had a prior COVID-19 infection, on top of being vaccinated, gives extra protection against reinfection or severe disease compared to vaccination alone.
confidenceSummary: Moderate evidence base. The claim rests on a reasonable number of direct studies with strong agreement, but the evidence base is still building and would benefit from more research across diverse populations and longer time periods.

guide.whatScienceSays: DATOM looked at 18 studies that directly tested this claim. Of those, 16 (89%) support the idea that a prior COVID-19 infection on top of vaccination gives extra protection against reinfection or severe disease compared with vaccination alone; 2 (11%) point the other way. So most of the clear findings back the claim, which is what the "Supported" verdict below means. But the Grade C beside it matters just as much: the evidence base is moderate in size and quality, so this is a reasonably solid result, though not yet definitive. Many more studies touched on the topic without testing this exact claim; they appear further down, tagged by what they looked at.
guide.howConfident:
The 89% support share is strong, and 18 decisive studies is a moderate-sized evidence base—enough to show a clear pattern but not yet large enough for the highest confidence. The Grade C reflects that this finding rests on a reasonable number of direct tests, with consistent results across most of them.

The gap between the raw support share and the grade comes down to study count and breadth. While nearly 9 in 10 studies agree, 18 total studies means the evidence base is still building. A larger body of work, especially with more diverse populations and longer follow-up periods, would push the grade higher even with the same support percentage.
decisionSupport: Sixteen out of 18 studies found that hybrid immunity—prior infection plus vaccination—provides stronger protection than vaccination alone.
The 89% support share shows a clear directional consensus across the decisive evidence base.
Only 2 studies out of 18 found results that contradicted the claim, indicating minimal counter-evidence.
The moderate evidence base of 18 decisive studies provides a reasonably solid foundation for the Supported verdict.
Additional studies in the corpus touched on related aspects of hybrid immunity without directly testing this specific comparison.
guide.faultLines:
Population differences: Some studies focused on specific age groups or health conditions, which may limit how broadly the findings apply to everyone. Protection levels could vary between healthy young adults and older or immunocompromised individuals.

Timing variables: The studies measured protection at different time points after infection and vaccination, making it hard to pin down exactly how long the extra protection lasts. Some measured outcomes weeks after vaccination, others many months later.

Variant context: Studies were conducted during different waves of the pandemic with different dominant variants, so the extra protection seen in one variant era might not match what happens with newer strains.
